title: Safety in Disclosure: An Integrated Model of Dyadic Disclosure of Marginalized Group Members Across Identities to Dominant Group Members
abstract: ABSTRACT Self‐disclosure is a well‐documented facilitator of positive intergroup contact. The present work adopts a dyadic perspective to integrate models of disclosure and responsiveness from two previously distinct literature: experience‐based disclosure in interracial interactions and identity disclosure among individuals with stigmatized identities. This integrated explanatory framework broadens the scope of prior models to encompass disclosure experiences across a wider range of contexts and marginalized groups—including members of racially minoritized groups, people with disabilities, and sexual minorities—during interactions with dominant group members. We first outline individual and contextual factors that shape marginalized group members' decision to disclose. Following their disclosure of an identity or identity‐related experience, we delineate intended and enacted responsiveness from dominant group members. We then highlight how the responsiveness of dominant group members informs marginalized group members' perceptions of responsiveness, and subsequent intrapersonal and relational outcomes. Likewise, we provide evidence of distinct outcomes for dominant group members following their response. Finally, we highlight how this framework can encourage novel insights and research, such as consideration for disclosure processes of people with intersectional identities. This approach illustrates how perceptions of both marginalized and dominant group members jointly shape disclosure, responsiveness, and outcomes across intergroup contexts.
